# F08 — Reviewer Certification Application

**AxiomDynamics LLC** · Form F08 · Version 1.0 · Effective ____________ · **Retain 7 years (plus certification life)**

**Purpose:** to apply for certification of a Customer employee to record advisory dispositions in the Platform.

**Governing reference:** C02 (Certification & Role-Based Assessment).

> **Why this form exists:** **since 2026-11-11 a certification ID can no longer be self-asserted at entry** — a disposition requires a local account bound to a live certification record, and the reviewer identity on the row comes from the authenticated session (B01 §7 item 1; D09 §4.4). What this form still does, and what the code does not, is establish **who the person behind that credential is**: issuing the credential, keeping custody of it, and withdrawing it on a mover or leaver. Entry additionally does not require an **attestation**, only a live session, so an attested row remains the reviewer's choice. **This form therefore stays the authoritative record of who is certified and who holds which credential** until key custody and joiner/mover/leaver are a running process. It is signed, filed, checked against the Platform's user list, and is the document from which an account and a registry key are issued. That manual control is what substitutes for the personnel control software cannot provide.

---

## Part 1 — Candidate

| | |
|---|---|
| Customer | |
| Site | |
| Candidate full name | |
| Employee ID | |
| Job title | |
| Department | |
| **Role applied for** | ☐ Operator ☐ Reviewer ☐ Administrator ☐ Safety Officer |
| Application date | |
| Nominated by (Customer sponsor) | |

---

## Part 2 — Eligibility (completed by the Customer sponsor)

**Reviewers must meet all of the following.** Confirm each:

☐ **At least 12 months of railroad operating, mechanical, or inspection experience** — years: ______
☐ Currently employed by the Customer in a role that touches rolling stock, track, or inspection
☐ Not under any disciplinary restriction affecting safety-critical duties
☐ Available to review advisories within the Customer's defined response window
☐ Willing to record dispositions in writing, including where the Platform is judged wrong

**Administrators must meet all of the following:**

☐ **At least 2 years of hands-on Linux system administration**
☐ Able to manage the host, the database, backups, and the NTP configuration
☐ Holds the Customer's internal authority to operate the Platform host

**Operators (read-only) require:**

☐ A business need to view advisories
☐ No disciplinary restriction

---

## Part 3 — Curriculum completion

| Module | Completed | Date | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Role and boundaries of a Reviewer (C02 §2) | ☐ | | |
| Reading an advisory: what the Platform computes | ☐ | | |
| The physics behind the ranked risk score | ☐ | | |
| Disposition discipline: recording reject, accept, defer | ☐ | | |
| What a Reviewer must **never** do (operating decisions, inspection substitution) | ☐ | | |
| Record keeping and the append-only ledger | ☐ | | |
| Escalation and the support boundary | ☐ | | |

**Assessment result:** ______ %  **Pass threshold:** **80%** (C02 §3.2)

---

## Part 4 — Assessment record

| | |
|---|---|
| Assessed by (AxiomDynamics) | |
| Assessment date | |
| Format | ☐ Written ☐ Practical ☐ Both |
| Result | ☐ **Pass** ☐ **Fail** — retake permitted after ______ |

---

## Part 5 — Critical acknowledgements

**The candidate must initial each line.** These are not boilerplate — each one is a specific boundary the candidate is being trusted with.

| Initial | Acknowledgement |
|---|---|
| ____ | I understand the Platform is a **decision-support tool**, not a certified safety appliance (D12). |
| ____ | I understand the Platform does **not** satisfy any WDBD or other regulatory inspection requirement (D12 §3). |
| ____ | I understand that **I**, not AxiomDynamics, make the operating decision. The Platform ranks risk; I decide what happens to the train. |
| ____ | I will **never** rely on the Platform as a substitute for a required inspection. |
| ____ | I will record a disposition for **every** advisory assigned to me, including where I judge the Platform to be wrong. |
| ____ | I will not ask AxiomDynamics personnel for operating advice, and I understand they will decline to give it (D06 §1.4). |
| ____ | I will record dispositions under my own name only, and will not share my credentials. |
| ____ | I understand my certification is **valid for three years**, with renewal on the three-year cycle (C02 §4.1). |
| ____ | I understand my certification may be **revoked** by the Customer or suspended by AxiomDynamics for misuse (Part 8). |

---

## Part 6 — Certification issued

| | |
|---|---|
| **Certificate number** | **CRT-______** |
| Role certified | |
| Issued date | |
| **Valid until** (3 years) | |
| **Renewal due** (year 2) | |
| Issued by (AxiomDynamics) | |

**Registry entry made:** ☐ Yes — date: __________  **Platform user account created:** ☐ Yes — username: __________

---

## Part 7 — What certification does and does not mean

**It means:** the holder completed the curriculum and passed an assessment against it. That is a statement about training.

**It does not mean:** that the holder will never make an error; that the holder is competent in every situation; that AxiomDynamics supervises or directs the holder's work; or that AxiomDynamics accepts liability for the holder's acts or omissions.

**The Customer remains solely responsible for the employment, supervision, and performance of its personnel** (D07 §16). Certification evidences curriculum completion and creates no liability for a Certified Reviewer's act (D07 §16).

---

## Part 8 — Revocation

Certification is revoked or suspended on:

1. Termination of the holder's employment with the Customer
2. Misuse of credentials or recording a disposition under another person's name

content.text:
Do this **once**, at commissioning, before any disposition is recorded, and again only when rotating the key under D09 §4.5. The export key is what lets the Railroad prove, later and without trusting the platform host, that the ledger it holds is the ledger that was written.

```bash
cd /opt/axiom/AxiomDynamics
# 1. Generate the signing key. It is written mode 0600, and it must never be
#    copied onto the platform host's backups or into the source tree.
python3 -m backend.ledger_export keygen --key-file /root/axiom-export.key

# 2. RECORD THE KEY_ID IT PRINTS in the custody log (D09 §4.5.2). Anyone
#    holding a bundle can compare its key_id to this figure.

# 3. Take a baseline export immediately.
python3 -m backend.ledger_export export \
    --key-file /root/axiom-export.key \
    --out /var/lib/axiom-export/ledger-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# 4. Verify it on a DIFFERENT machine that has neither the database nor this
#    checkout -- the whole point is that verification does not need them.
python3 tools/verify_ledger_export.py \
    --key-file /path/to/copied/key \
    --bundle ledger-20261109.json

"""
Tests for tools/pin_requirements.py (D09 §4.4 hash pinning).

The failure this suite is written against is not "the tool crashes". It is the
one that nearly shipped: **a digest written by a human, or by a model, into a
file that therefore looks pinned and is not.** `pip install --require-hashes`
rejects a wrong hash, so the control fails closed — but it fails at release time,
on the Railroad's machine, after the artefact was shipped. The tests below pin
down that the tool can only ever write a hash it observed in the same run.

Nothing here touches the network. The download step is exercised with fakes,
because a suite that needs PyPI to run is a suite that does not run on the
air-gapped box this product is built for.

Run: python3 -I tests/test_pin_requirements.py
"""

import importlib.util
import os
import sys
import tempfile

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
sys.path.insert(0, ROOT)

TOOL = os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "pin_requirements.py")
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("pin_requirements", TOOL)
pin = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(pin)

RESULTS = []


def test(fn):
    try:
        fn()
    except AssertionError as exc:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, exc))
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, "%s: %s" % (type(exc).__name__, exc)))

"""
Tests for tools/issue_reviewer_key.py (D09 §8.4.2, the joiner step).

The failure this suite is written against is not "the script crashes". It is a
credential issue that *appears* to succeed and leaves the reviewer unable to
attest, or leaves two copies of a key where there should be one:

  * a key file written for a registration the registry refused — bytes on disk
    that no registry entry names, and that will be walked past by a later run;
  * an existing key file overwritten, destroying the only copy of a credential
    that an append-only registry cannot re-register once revoked.

Each is tested by driving the real CLI, not by re-implementing it.

Run: python3 -I tests/test_issue_reviewer_key.py
"""

import importlib.util
import os
import stat
import sys
import tempfile

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
sys.path.insert(0, ROOT)

TOOL = os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "issue_reviewer_key.py")
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("issue_reviewer_key", TOOL)
issue = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(issue)

RESULTS = []


def test(fn):
    try:
        fn()
    except AssertionError as exc:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, exc))
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, "%s: %s" % (type(exc).__name__, exc)))
    else:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, True, None))
    return fn


class _Tmp:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        self.db = os.path.join(self.d, "t.db")
        return self

    def path(self, name):
        return os.path.join(self.d, name)

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        import shutil
        shutil.rmtree(self.d, ignore_errors=True)
        return False


@test
def test_it_writes_a_32_byte_key_mode_0600_and_registers_it():
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("hoffman.key")
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                         "--key-file", kf, "--db", t.db])
        assert rc == 0, rc
        with open(kf, "rb") as fh:
            key = fh.read()
        assert len(key) == 32, len(key)
        mode = stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(kf).st_mode)
        assert mode == 0o600, oct(mode)

        from backend import attribution
        rows = attribution.registry(t.db)
        assert len(rows) == 1, rows
        assert rows[0]["reviewer"] == "Hoffman", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["cert_id"] == "CERT-H-1", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["key_id"] == attribution.key_id(key), rows[0]


@test
def test_it_refuses_to_overwrite_an_existing_key_file():
    # A key file is the only copy of a credential. Overwriting it would leave a
    # registry entry whose bytes are gone, and the registry is append-only.
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("hoffman.key")
        with open(kf, "wb") as fh:
            fh.write(b"x" * 32)
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                         "--key-file", kf, "--db", t.db])
        assert rc == 2, "overwrite must be refused with rc 2, got %r" % (rc,)
        with open(kf, "rb") as fh:
            assert fh.read() == b"x" * 32, "the existing key file was modified"


@test
def test_a_refused_registration_leaves_no_key_file():
    # Register Okafor with a key, then try to register the *same* reviewer name
    # under a certificate that will be refused for a different reason: a
    # database that cannot be opened. The observable is the key file.
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("orphan.key")
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "X", "--cert", "C",
                         "--key-file", kf,
                         "--db", os.path.join(t.d, "no", "such", "dir.db")])
        assert rc != 0, "a failed registration must not report success"
        assert not os.path.exists(kf), \
            "a key file was written for a registration that was refused"


@test
def test_two_reviewers_get_distinct_keys():
    with _Tmp() as t:
        a = t.path("a.key")
        b = t.path("b.key")
        assert issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                           "--key-file", a, "--db", t.db]) == 0
        assert issue.main(["--reviewer", "Okafor", "--cert", "CERT-O-1",
                           "--key-file", b, "--db", t.db]) == 0
        with open(a, "rb") as fh:
            ka = fh.read()
        with open(b, "rb") as fh:
            kb = fh.read()
        assert ka != kb, "two reviewers were issued the same key bytes"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    passed = sum(1 for _, ok, _ in RESULTS if ok)
    failed = len(RESULTS) - passed
    for name, ok, exc in RESULTS:
        print(("PASS  " if ok else "FAIL  ") + name + ("" if ok else " -> %s" % exc))
    print("\n%d passed, %d failed" % (passed, failed))
    sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)

"""
Tests for tools/issue_reviewer_key.py (D09 §8.4.2, the joiner step).

The failure this suite is written against is not "the script crashes". It is a
credential issue that *appears* to succeed and leaves the reviewer unable to
attest, or leaves two copies of a key where there should be one:

  * a key file written for a registration the registry refused — bytes on disk
    that no registry entry names, and that will be walked past by a later run;
  * an existing key file overwritten, destroying the only copy of a credential
    that an append-only registry cannot re-register once revoked.

Each is tested by driving the real CLI, not by re-implementing it.

Run: python3 -I tests/test_issue_reviewer_key.py
"""

import importlib.util
import os
import stat
import sys
import tempfile

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
sys.path.insert(0, ROOT)

TOOL = os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "issue_reviewer_key.py")
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("issue_reviewer_key", TOOL)
issue = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(issue)

RESULTS = []


def test(fn):
    try:
        fn()
    except AssertionError as exc:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, exc))
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, "%s: %s" % (type(exc).__name__, exc)))
    else:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, True, None))
    return fn


class _Tmp:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        self.db = os.path.join(self.d, "t.db")
        return self

    def path(self, name):
        return os.path.join(self.d, name)

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        import shutil
        shutil.rmtree(self.d, ignore_errors=True)
        return False


@test
def test_it_writes_a_32_byte_key_mode_0600_and_registers_it():
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("hoffman.key")
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                         "--key-file", kf, "--db", t.db])
        assert rc == 0, rc
        with open(kf, "rb") as fh:
            key = fh.read()
        assert len(key) == 32, len(key)
        mode = stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(kf).st_mode)
        assert mode == 0o600, oct(mode)

        from backend import attribution
        rows = attribution.registry(t.db)
        assert len(rows) == 1, rows
        assert rows[0]["reviewer"] == "Hoffman", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["cert_id"] == "CERT-H-1", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["key_id"] == attribution.key_id(key), rows[0]

def test_it_refuses_to_overwrite_an_existing_key_file():

    # registry entry whose bytes are gone, and the registry is append-only.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Issue a reviewer credential: generate the key, register it, print the key_id.

This is the joiner step in D09 §8.4.2. It exists because that procedure named
an action nobody could perform — a reviewer key could only be created by
`tools/seed_demo_account.py`, which generates one and *discards it* (correctly:
printing a demo key would be the worst thing that script could do). A procedure
that cannot be carried out is not a control, so the missing piece is here.

What it does, in order, because the second refuses unless the first succeeded:

  1. generate 32 bytes from the OS CSPRNG and write them mode 0600;
  2. register the key against a reviewer and certificate (`attribution.register`);
  3. print the `key_id` for the custody log (D09 §8.4.6) — **never the key**.

The certificate must already exist in the registry or be created by this call:
`register` binds the key to a `cert_id`, and `accounts.enroll` later refuses an
account whose certificate is not live. Registering the certificate is part of
issuing the credential, so this tool does both by default.

Usage::

    python3 -I tools/issue_reviewer_key.py \\
        --reviewer "Hoffman" --cert CERT-H-1 --key-file /secure/hoffman.key

The certificate is registered by this call. Registering the key is not
optional and has no separate switch: an unregistered key attests nothing.

**The key file is written to a path you choose and is not backed up for you.**
That is deliberate: D09 §8.4.1 forbids storing it beside the bundles it signs or
on the export media. Move it to the reviewer's custody, or the Railroad's
sealed store, and record where in the custody log.

Refuses to overwrite an existing key file. A silent overwrite here destroys the
only copy of a credential, and the registry cannot be repaired afterwards.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import secrets
import stat
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))


def _write_secret(path: str, key: bytes) -> None:
    """Create `path` exclusively, mode 0600, and write the key."""
    # O_EXCL so a second run cannot destroy the first key. The registry forbids
    # re-registering revoked bytes, but a lost key is not recoverable even if
    # the registry entry survives.
    fd = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600)
    try:
        os.write(fd, key)
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.chmod(path, stat.S_IRUSR | stat.S_IWUSR)


def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[1])
    ap.add_argument("--reviewer", required=True,
                    help="display name the key attributes; one reviewer per key")
    ap.add_argument("--cert", required=True,
                    help="certificate ID the key is bound to")
    ap.add_argument("--key-file", required=True,
                    help="where to write the 32-byte key (mode 0600, must not exist)")
    ap.add_argument("--note", default="", help="registry note, e.g. the F08 reference")
    ap.add_argument("--db", default=None,
                    help="axiom.db path; defaults to the Platform's own")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    from backend import attribution, store

    db = args.db or store.DB_PATH

    if os.path.exists(args.key_file):
        print("refusing to overwrite %s — a key file is the only copy of a "
              "credential. Move it aside or choose another path."
              % args.key_file, file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    key = secrets.token_bytes(32)
    try:
        entry = attribution.register(db, args.reviewer, args.cert, key,
                                     note=args.note)
    except ValueError as exc:
        # Nothing was written; do not leave a key file behind for a key the
        # registry refused.
        print("register: %s" % exc, file=sys.stderr)
        print("\nNo key file was written.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    try:
        _write_secret(args.key_file, key)
    except OSError as exc:
        # The registry entry now exists and cannot be removed. That is a real
        # problem and must be reported rather than swallowed: revoke the
        # registration for cause (it has no usable key file) and issue again.
        print("WARNING: %s registered %r under %s, but the key file could not "
              "be written (%s)." % (entry["key_id"], args.reviewer,
                                    args.cert, exc), file=sys.stderr)
        print("Revoke this registration (attribution.revoke) and issue a new "
              "key — the registered bytes exist only in this process and are "
              "about to be lost.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 3

    kid = attribution.key_id(key)
    print("issued       %r under %s" % (args.reviewer, args.cert))
    print("key_id       %s" % kid)
    print("key file     %s (mode 0600)" % args.key_file)
    print("\nRecord in the custody log (D09 §8.4.6) — date, 'joined', reviewer,")
    print("certificate, key_id %s, where the file is held, and who issued it." % kid)
    print("Do NOT record the key itself anywhere.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# AD-2 key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — 2026-11-11

Internal build record. Chat-8, phase two. The docket document is **D09 §8.4**;
this is why it says what it says and what writing it turned up.

## What was asked

B01 §7 item 1 has been open on "key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — a written
procedure, not code" since chat-6. Chat-7 narrowed it further with the signed
key directory. The instruction was to write the procedure.

## Where it went, and why not a new document

D09 is the security addendum and already had §4.5 for the **export** key's
custody. It also had §8.1–8.3 on access control, which were thin: 8.2 said
"the Railroad revokes their Platform access" and stopped. A reviewer credential
is the same class of problem as an export key, so the procedure belongs beside
the one the docket already carries. **§8.4, eight subsections.** No new document
and no new docket ID — adding an artifact for a procedure the security addendum
is the natural home for would have meant a new ID for content that belongs to an
existing one.

## What the section says

**8.4.1** separates the three credentials, because conflating them is how this
fails in practice: an account (passphrase, PBKDF2 verifier), a session token
(32 bytes, digest stored, transient), and a reviewer attestation key (32 raw
bytes, `key_id` published, key held). It says plainly that the attestation key
is not a password — losing it stops attesting, not signing in.

**8.4.2–8.4.5** are joiner, mover, leaver and rotation, each fixed in order
because each step depends on the one before. The joiner begins at a signed F08
and cannot begin anywhere else, since an account is bound to a certificate that
must already be live.

**8.4.4** is the load-bearing one. It splits the leaver path into what the
software does and what a person must do: revoking the certificate **immediately
stops every live session bound to it**, because `resolve_session` re-checks
liveness at each call; revoking the account and handling the key are manual.

**8.4.6** adds the custody log — the Railroad's human register, recording
`key_id` and never the key, which is the only record that ties a key to a person
rather than to a certificate.

**8.4.7** forbids using the export key as a reviewer key or the reverse.

**8.4.8** states the limits: a credential holder is not a person; the scheme is
symmetric; a demo cannot attest; and nothing but revocation is enforced by
software.

## What writing it turned up

**Two real defects, both found by trying to make the procedure's own sentences
true.** This is the part worth carrying: neither was found by a test, and one
had been in the code since chat-6 and survived a suite of 346 tests plus two
adversarial audits.

### 1. A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won

I wrote "`attribution.register` refuses a key already registered under a
different reviewer". Before publishing the sentence I ran it. It did not.

`register` refused only a key revoked *anywhere* in its history. A *live* key
presented under a different reviewer was accepted. Because `attest` resolves the
**newest** registry entry for a `key_id` — deliberately, so a certificate
renewal works — the second reviewer took the key over: they could attest rows
naming themselves, and the original reviewer was locked out of their own key.

The registry is append-only, so the bad binding **could never be removed**. The
key directory caught the conflict at publish time (`entries_consistent`), which
is far too late to be useful: the register is already poisoned.

Fixed in `register`, at the write. Verified against both sides:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Same key, different reviewer | accepted, key hijacked | **refused** |
| Same key, same reviewer, same cert | accepted | accepted |
| Same key, same reviewer, **renewed** cert | accepted | accepted |

The second and third matter: renewal is the documented path in §8.4.5 and
`test_a_renewal_under_a_new_certificate_exports_the_new_certificate` depends on
it. My first attempt refused the renewal too, which would have broken rotation
to fix a sharing bug. The rule is about the **reviewer** changing, not the
certificate.

### 2. A refused key directory still handed back bindings

`key_directory.verify` returned `{"ok": False, "bindings": {"<key>": "Hoffman"}}`
for a directory it had just refused for naming one key two reviewers. The
refusal was true and the conflicted name was still on offer — anything that
checks `ok` late, or logs the bindings and carries on, took a name from a
document that had failed.

Fixed: a refused directory returns `{}`. Tested from both directions, so the fix
cannot empty the happy path.

### 3. The procedure named a tool that did not exist

§8.4.2 initially said to call `attribution.register(...)`. There was no way for
an operator to do that: the only code that created a reviewer key was
`tools/seed_demo_account.py`, and it **generates a key and discards it** — so on
a demo nobody holds a key and attestation can never happen (now disclosed in
§8.4.8 rather than left as a silent absence).

`tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the missing piece: generate, register, print
the `key_id`, never the key. It refuses to overwrite an existing key file,
because a key file is the only copy of a credential and the registry cannot be
repaired after the fact. **4 tests**, including that a refused registration
leaves no key file behind — bytes on disk that no registry entry names are how a
later run silently issues a second credential.

## Verification

Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about:

- A session issued, then its certificate revoked → the next resolve fails with
  *"the certification behind this session has been revoked"*.
- A revoked account cannot be re-enrolled under the same username, which is why
  §8.4.3 says a mover's account is **not** revoked.
- `attribution.revoke` and `accounts.revoke_account` both exist with those names.
- `ledger_export.py keygen` runs, writes mode 0600, and prints the `key_id` §4.5.1
  says it prints.
- The C01 command as written in the docket runs and issues a key.

Both new guards are mutation-tested: removing the reviewer guard fails exactly
`test_one_key_cannot_be_registered_to_a_second_reviewer`; restoring the leaked
bindings fails exactly `test_a_refused_directory_returns_no_bindings`.

Suite **351 → 359**: 2 attribution, 2 key-directory, 4 for the tool.

## Docket corrected in the same pass

B01 §10 (AD-2 bullet), §2 item 2, §7 item 1 (status cell and its closing
paragraph), B02 §2, C01 (new reviewer-credential block), C02 §5, D00 Part IV and
the AD-2 line, D09 §4.4 rows, and F08's preamble. Grep confirms no document
still claims the procedure is unwritten.

## Not closed, and the section says so

A credential holder is not a person; the HMAC scheme is symmetric; a demo cannot
attest; and every step except certificate revocation is performed by a human.
Writing the procedure makes the item **auditable** under D09 §10.1, which is a
real change — but it is not the same as closing it, and B01 §7 item 1 now says
exactly that rather than implying a document settles the matter.

Write the AD-2 custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure (D09 §8.4)

B01 §7 item 1 has been open on "key custody and joiner/mover/leaver - a
written procedure, not code". This writes it, in D09 beside §4.5, which already
does the same job for the export key.

Writing the procedure down forced three things the code did not support, and
none of them was found by a test.

1. A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won.
   `register` refused only a key revoked anywhere in its history; a *live* key
   presented under a different reviewer was accepted. Since `attest` resolves
   the newest entry for a key_id - deliberately, so a renewal works - the
   second reviewer took the key over: they could attest rows naming
   themselves, and the original holder was locked out of their own key. The
   register is append-only, so the bad binding could never be removed, and the
   key directory caught it only at publish time. Now refused at the write.
   A renewal under a new certificate for the *same* reviewer still works,
   which §8.4.5 and an existing test both depend on.

2. A refused key directory still handed back bindings. verify() returned
   ok=False with bindings={'<key>': 'Hoffman'} for the very directory it had
   refused for naming one key two reviewers. A caller that checks ok late, or
   logs the bindings and carries on, took a name from a failed document.
   A refused directory now returns no bindings.

3. The procedure named a step nobody could perform. The only code that created
   a reviewer key was seed_demo_account.py, which generates one and discards
   it - so on a demo no key exists and attestation can never happen (now stated
   in §8.4.8). tools/issue_reviewer_key.py is the missing joiner step:
   generate, register, print the key_id and never the key, refusing to
   overwrite an existing key file.

Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about: a
revoked certificate stops a live session at the next resolve; a revoked account
cannot be re-enrolled under the same username (hence a mover's account is not
revoked); keygen writes 0600 and prints the key_id; the C01 command runs.

Both new guards are mutation-tested - each fails exactly one test when removed,
and no other. Suite 351 -> 359.

Docket corrected in the same pass: B01 §2/§7 item 1/§10, B02 §2, C01, C02 §5,
D00 Part IV, D09 §4.4, F08. Item 1 is not closed: a credential holder is not a
person, the scheme is symmetric, and every step but revocation is done by a
human. What changed is that the item is now auditable under D09 §10.1, and the
documents say that rather than implying a procedure settles the matter.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

# AD-2 key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — 2026-11-11

Internal build record. Chat-8, phase two. The docket document is **D09 §8.4**;
this is why it says what it says and what writing it turned up.

## What was asked

B01 §7 item 1 has been open on "key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — a written
procedure, not code" since chat-6. Chat-7 narrowed it further with the signed
key directory. The instruction was to write the procedure.

## Where it went, and why not a new document

D09 is the security addendum and already had §4.5 for the **export** key's
custody. It also had §8.1–8.3 on access control, which were thin: 8.2 said
"the Railroad revokes their Platform access" and stopped. A reviewer credential
is the same class of problem as an export key, so the procedure belongs beside
the one the docket already carries. **§8.4, eight subsections.** No new document
and no new docket ID — adding an artifact for a procedure the security addendum
is the natural home for would have meant a new ID for content that belongs to an
existing one.

## What the section says

**8.4.1** separates the three credentials, because conflating them is how this
fails in practice: an account (passphrase, PBKDF2 verifier), a session token
(32 bytes, digest stored, transient), and a reviewer attestation key (32 raw
bytes, `key_id` published, key held). It says plainly that the attestation key
is not a password — losing it stops attesting, not signing in.

**8.4.2–8.4.5** are joiner, mover, leaver and rotation, each fixed in order
because each step depends on the one before. The joiner begins at a signed F08
and cannot begin anywhere else, since an account is bound to a certificate that
must already be live.

**8.4.4** is the load-bearing one. It splits the leaver path into what the
software does and what a person must do: revoking the certificate **immediately
stops every live session bound to it**, because `resolve_session` re-checks
liveness at each call; revoking the account and handling the key are manual.

**8.4.6** adds the custody log — the Railroad's human register, recording
`key_id` and never the key, which is the only record that ties a key to a person
rather than to a certificate.

**8.4.7** forbids using the export key as a reviewer key or the reverse.

**8.4.8** states the limits: a credential holder is not a person; the scheme is
symmetric; a demo cannot attest; and nothing but revocation is enforced by
software.

## What writing it turned up

**Two real defects, both found by trying to make the procedure's own sentences
true.** This is the part worth carrying: neither was found by a test, and one
had been in the code since chat-6 and survived a suite of 346 tests plus two
adversarial audits.

### 1. A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won

I wrote "`attribution.register` refuses a key already registered under a
different reviewer". Before publishing the sentence I ran it. It did not.

`register` refused only a key revoked *anywhere* in its history. A *live* key
presented under a different reviewer was accepted. Because `attest` resolves the
**newest** registry entry for a `key_id` — deliberately, so a certificate
renewal works — the second reviewer took the key over: they could attest rows
naming themselves, and the original reviewer was locked out of their own key.

The registry is append-only, so the bad binding **could never be removed**. The
key directory caught the conflict at publish time (`entries_consistent`), which
is far too late to be useful: the register is already poisoned.

Fixed in `register`, at the write. Verified against both sides:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Same key, different reviewer | accepted, key hijacked | **refused** |
| Same key, same reviewer, same cert | accepted | accepted |
| Same key, same reviewer, **renewed** cert | accepted | accepted |

The second and third matter: renewal is the documented path in §8.4.5 and
`test_a_renewal_under_a_new_certificate_exports_the_new_certificate` depends on
it. My first attempt refused the renewal too, which would have broken rotation
to fix a sharing bug. The rule is about the **reviewer** changing, not the
certificate.

### 2. A refused key directory still handed back bindings

`key_directory.verify` returned `{"ok": False, "bindings": {"<key>": "Hoffman"}}`
for a directory it had just refused for naming one key two reviewers. The
refusal was true and the conflicted name was still on offer — anything that
checks `ok` late, or logs the bindings and carries on, took a name from a
document that had failed.

Fixed: a refused directory returns `{}`. Tested from both directions, so the fix
cannot empty the happy path.

### 3. The procedure named a tool that did not exist

§8.4.2 initially said to call `attribution.register(...)`. There was no way for
an operator to do that: the only code that created a reviewer key was
`tools/seed_demo_account.py`, and it **generates a key and discards it** — so on
a demo nobody holds a key and attestation can never happen (now disclosed in
§8.4.8 rather than left as a silent absence).

`tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the missing piece: generate, register, print
the `key_id`, never the key. It refuses to overwrite an existing key file,
because a key file is the only copy of a credential and the registry cannot be
repaired after the fact. **4 tests**, including that a refused registration
leaves no key file behind — bytes on disk that no registry entry names are how a
later run silently issues a second credential.

## Verification

Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about:

- A session issued, then its certificate revoked → the next resolve fails with
  *"the certification behind this session has been revoked"*.
- A revoked account cannot be re-enrolled under the same username, which is why
  §8.4.3 says a mover's account is **not** revoked.
- `attribution.revoke` and `accounts.revoke_account` both exist with those names.
- `ledger_export.py keygen` runs, writes mode 0600, and prints the `key_id` §4.5.1
  says it prints.
- The C01 command as written in the docket runs and issues a key.

Both new guards are mutation-tested: removing the reviewer guard fails exactly
`test_one_key_cannot_be_registered_to_a_second_reviewer`; restoring the leaked
bindings fails exactly `test_a_refused_directory_returns_no_bindings`.

Suite **351 → 359**: 2 attribution, 2 key-directory, 4 for the tool.

## Docket corrected in the same pass

B01 §10 (AD-2 bullet), §2 item 2, §7 item 1 (status cell and its closing
paragraph), B02 §2, C01 (new reviewer-credential block), C02 §5, D00 Part IV and
the AD-2 line, D09 §4.4 rows, and F08's preamble. Grep confirms no document
still claims the procedure is unwritten.

## Not closed, and the section says so

A credential holder is not a person; the HMAC scheme is symmetric; a demo cannot
attest; and every step except certificate revocation is performed by a human.
Writing the procedure makes the item **auditable** under D09 §10.1, which is a
real change — but it is not the same as closing it, and B01 §7 item 1 now says
exactly that rather than implying a document settles the matter.

66	renewal works — the second reviewer took the key over: they could attest rows
67	naming themselves, and the original reviewer was locked out of their own key.
68	
69	The registry is append-only, so the bad binding **could never be removed**. The
70	key directory caught the conflict at publish time (`entries_consistent`), which
71	is far too late to be useful: the register is already poisoned.
72	
73	Fixed in `register`, at the write. Verified against both sides:
74	
75	| Case | Before | After |
76	|---|---|---|
77	| Same key, different reviewer | accepted, key hijacked | **refused** |
78	| Same key, same reviewer, same cert | accepted | accepted |
79	| Same key, same reviewer, **renewed** cert | accepted | accepted |
80	
81	The second and third matter: renewal is the documented path in §8.4.5 and
82	`test_a_renewal_under_a_new_certificate_exports_the_new_certificate` depends on
83	it. My first attempt refused the renewal too, which would have broken rotation
84	to fix a sharing bug. The rule is about the **reviewer** changing, not the
85	certificate.
86	
87	### 2. A refused key directory still handed back bindings
88	
89	`key_directory.verify` returned `{"ok": False, "bindings": {"<key>": "Hoffman"}}`
90	for a directory it had just refused for naming one key two reviewers. The
91	refusal was true and the conflicted name was still on offer — anything that
92	checks `ok` late, or logs the bindings and carries on, took a name from a
93	document that had failed.
94	
95	Fixed: a refused directory returns `{}`. Tested from both directions, so the fix
96	cannot empty the happy path.
97	
98	### 3. The procedure named a tool that did not exist
99	
100	§8.4.2 initially said to call `attribution.register(...)`. There was no way for
101	an operator to do that: the only code that created a reviewer key was
102	`tools/seed_demo_account.py`, and it **generates a key and discards it** — so on
103	a demo nobody holds a key and attestation can never happen (now disclosed in
104	§8.4.8 rather than left as a silent absence).
105	
106	`tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the missing piece: generate, register, print
107	the `key_id`, never the key. It refuses to overwrite an existing key file,
108	because a key file is the only copy of a credential and the registry cannot be
109	repaired after the fact. **4 tests**, including that a refused registration
110	leaves no key file behind — bytes on disk that no registry entry names are how a
111	later run silently issues a second credential.
112	
113	## Verification
114	
115	Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about:
116	
117	- A session issued, then its certificate revoked → the next resolve fails with
118	  *"the certification behind this session has been revoked"*.
119	- A revoked account cannot be re-enrolled under the same username, which is why
120	  §8.4.3 says a mover's account is **not** revoked.
121	- `attribution.revoke` and `accounts.revoke_account` both exist with those names.
122	- `ledger_export.py keygen` runs, writes mode 0600, and prints the `key_id` §4.5.1
123	  says it prints.
124	- The C01 command as written in the docket runs and issues a key.
125	
126	Both new guards are mutation-tested: removing the reviewer guard fails exactly
127	`test_one_key_cannot_be_registered_to_a_second_reviewer`; restoring the leaked
128	bindings fails exactly `test_a_refused_directory_returns_no_bindings`.
129	
130	Suite **351 → 359**: 2 attribution, 2 key-directory, 4 for the tool.
131	
132	## Docket corrected in the same pass
133	
134	B01 §10 (AD-2 bullet), §2 item 2, §7 item 1 (status cell and its closing
135	paragraph), B02 §2, C01 (new reviewer-credential block), C02 §5, D00 Part IV and
136	the AD-2 line, D09 §4.4 rows, and F08's preamble. Grep confirms no document
137	still claims the procedure is unwritten.
138	
139	## Not closed, and the section says so
140	
141	A credential holder is not a person; the HMAC scheme is symmetric; a demo cannot
142	attest; and every step except certificate revocation is performed by a human.
143	Writing the procedure makes the item **auditable** under D09 §10.1, which is a
144	real change — but it is not the same as closing it, and B01 §7 item 1 now says
145	exactly that rather than implying a document settles the matter.
146	
</system-reminder>

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Issue a reviewer credential: generate the key, register it, print the key_id.

This is the joiner step in D09 §8.4.2. It exists because that procedure named
an action nobody could perform — a reviewer key could only be created by
`tools/seed_demo_account.py`, which generates one and *discards it* (correctly:
printing a demo key would be the worst thing that script could do). A procedure
that cannot be carried out is not a control, so the missing piece is here.

What it does, in order, because the second refuses unless the first succeeded:

  1. generate 32 bytes from the OS CSPRNG and write them mode 0600;
  2. register the key against a reviewer and certificate (`attribution.register`);
  3. print the `key_id` for the custody log (D09 §8.4.6) — **never the key**.

The certificate must already exist in the registry or be created by this call:
`register` binds the key to a `cert_id`, and `accounts.enroll` later refuses an
account whose certificate is not live. Registering the certificate is part of
issuing the credential, so this tool does both by default.

Usage::

    python3 -I tools/issue_reviewer_key.py \\
        --reviewer "Hoffman" --cert CERT-H-1 --key-file /secure/hoffman.key

The certificate is registered by this call. Registering the key is not
optional and has no separate switch: an unregistered key attests nothing.

**The key file is written to a path you choose and is not backed up for you.**
That is deliberate: D09 §8.4.1 forbids storing it beside the bundles it signs or
on the export media. Move it to the reviewer's custody, or the Railroad's
sealed store, and record where in the custody log.

Refuses to overwrite an existing key file. A silent overwrite here destroys the
only copy of a credential, and the registry cannot be repaired afterwards.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import secrets
import stat
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))


def _write_secret(path: str, key: bytes) -> None:
    """Create `path` exclusively, mode 0600, and write the key."""
    # O_EXCL so a second run cannot destroy the first key. The registry forbids
    # re-registering revoked bytes, but a lost key is not recoverable even if
    # the registry entry survives.
    fd = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600)
    try:
        os.write(fd, key)
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.chmod(path, stat.S_IRUSR | stat.S_IWUSR)


def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[1])
    ap.add_argument("--reviewer", required=True,
                    help="display name the key attributes; one reviewer per key")
    ap.add_argument("--cert", required=True,
                    help="certificate ID the key is bound to")
    ap.add_argument("--key-file", required=True,
                    help="where to write the 32-byte key (mode 0600, must not exist)")
    ap.add_argument("--note", default="", help="registry note, e.g. the F08 reference")
    ap.add_argument("--db", default=None,
                    help="axiom.db path; defaults to the Platform's own")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    from backend import attribution, store

    db = args.db or store.DB_PATH

    if os.path.exists(args.key_file):
        print("refusing to overwrite %s — a key file is the only copy of a "
              "credential. Move it aside or choose another path."
              % args.key_file, file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    key = secrets.token_bytes(32)
    try:
        entry = attribution.register(db, args.reviewer, args.cert, key,
                                     note=args.note)
    except ValueError as exc:
        # Nothing was written; do not leave a key file behind for a key the
        # registry refused.
        print("register: %s" % exc, file=sys.stderr)
        print("\nNo key file was written.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        # An unopenable database, a locked file, a permissions problem. The
        # operator needs a refusal, not a traceback — and they need to know no
        # key file was written, which is the thing they would otherwise have to
        # check by looking.
        print("register failed: %s: %s" % (type(exc).__name__, exc),
              file=sys.stderr)
        print("\nNo key file was written.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    try:
        _write_secret(args.key_file, key)
    except OSError as exc:
        # The registry entry now exists and cannot be removed. That is a real
        # problem and must be reported rather than swallowed: revoke the
        # registration for cause (it has no usable key file) and issue again.
        print("WARNING: %s registered %r under %s, but the key file could not "
              "be written (%s)." % (entry["key_id"], args.reviewer,
                                    args.cert, exc), file=sys.stderr)
        print("Revoke this registration (attribution.revoke) and issue a new "
              "key — the registered bytes exist only in this process and are "
              "about to be lost.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 3

    kid = attribution.key_id(key)
    print("issued       %r under %s" % (args.reviewer, args.cert))
    print("key_id       %s" % kid)
    print("key file     %s (mode 0600)" % args.key_file)
    print("\nRecord in the custody log (D09 §8.4.6) — date, 'joined', reviewer,")
    print("certificate, key_id %s, where the file is held, and who issued it." % kid)
    print("Do NOT record the key itself anywhere.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""
Tests for tools/issue_reviewer_key.py (D09 §8.4.2, the joiner step).

The failure this suite is written against is not "the script crashes". It is a
credential issue that *appears* to succeed and leaves the reviewer unable to
attest, or leaves two copies of a key where there should be one:

  * a key file written for a registration the registry refused — bytes on disk
    that no registry entry names, and that will be walked past by a later run;
  * an existing key file overwritten, destroying the only copy of a credential
    that an append-only registry cannot re-register once revoked.

Each is tested by driving the real CLI, not by re-implementing it.

Run: python3 -I tests/test_issue_reviewer_key.py
"""

import importlib.util
import os
import stat
import sys
import tempfile

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
sys.path.insert(0, ROOT)

TOOL = os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "issue_reviewer_key.py")
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("issue_reviewer_key", TOOL)
issue = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(issue)

RESULTS = []


def test(fn):
    try:
        fn()
    except AssertionError as exc:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, exc))
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, False, "%s: %s" % (type(exc).__name__, exc)))
    else:
        RESULTS.append((fn.__name__, True, None))
    return fn


class _Tmp:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        self.db = os.path.join(self.d, "t.db")
        return self

    def path(self, name):
        return os.path.join(self.d, name)

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        import shutil
        shutil.rmtree(self.d, ignore_errors=True)
        return False


@test
def test_it_writes_a_32_byte_key_mode_0600_and_registers_it():
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("hoffman.key")
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                         "--key-file", kf, "--db", t.db])
        assert rc == 0, rc
        with open(kf, "rb") as fh:
            key = fh.read()
        assert len(key) == 32, len(key)
        mode = stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(kf).st_mode)
        assert mode == 0o600, oct(mode)

        from backend import attribution
        rows = attribution.registry(t.db)
        assert len(rows) == 1, rows
        assert rows[0]["reviewer"] == "Hoffman", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["cert_id"] == "CERT-H-1", rows[0]
        assert rows[0]["key_id"] == attribution.key_id(key), rows[0]


@test
def test_it_refuses_to_overwrite_an_existing_key_file():
    # A key file is the only copy of a credential. Overwriting it would leave a
    # registry entry whose bytes are gone, and the registry is append-only.
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("hoffman.key")
        with open(kf, "wb") as fh:
            fh.write(b"x" * 32)
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                         "--key-file", kf, "--db", t.db])
        assert rc == 2, "overwrite must be refused with rc 2, got %r" % (rc,)
        with open(kf, "rb") as fh:
            assert fh.read() == b"x" * 32, "the existing key file was modified"


@test
def test_a_refused_registration_leaves_no_key_file():
    # Register Okafor with a key, then try to register the *same* reviewer name
    # under a certificate that will be refused for a different reason: a
    # database that cannot be opened. The observable is the key file.
    with _Tmp() as t:
        kf = t.path("orphan.key")
        rc = issue.main(["--reviewer", "X", "--cert", "C",
                         "--key-file", kf,
                         "--db", os.path.join(t.d, "no", "such", "dir.db")])
        assert rc != 0, "a failed registration must not report success"
        assert not os.path.exists(kf), \
            "a key file was written for a registration that was refused"


@test
def test_two_reviewers_get_distinct_keys():
    with _Tmp() as t:
        a = t.path("a.key")
        b = t.path("b.key")
        assert issue.main(["--reviewer", "Hoffman", "--cert", "CERT-H-1",
                           "--key-file", a, "--db", t.db]) == 0
        assert issue.main(["--reviewer", "Okafor", "--cert", "CERT-O-1",
                           "--key-file", b, "--db", t.db]) == 0
        with open(a, "rb") as fh:
            ka = fh.read()
        with open(b, "rb") as fh:
            kb = fh.read()
        assert ka != kb, "two reviewers were issued the same key bytes"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    passed = sum(1 for _, ok, _ in RESULTS if ok)
    failed = len(RESULTS) - passed
    for name, ok, exc in RESULTS:
        print(("PASS  " if ok else "FAIL  ") + name + ("" if ok else " -> %s" % exc))
    print("\n%d passed, %d failed" % (passed, failed))
    sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)

## Scheduled tasks

The `mcp__scheduled-tasks__create_scheduled_task` tool sets up work that runs automatically — on a repeating schedule (every morning, weekly, hourly) or once at a specific future time (tomorrow at 3pm, in an hour).

**Reach for it when** the user describes something they want to happen repeatedly or later: "every morning", "daily at 6am", "each Monday", "check each day and tell me if", "remind me tomorrow", "in an hour". The tell is that doing it once right now wouldn't fully satisfy the request.

**Don't schedule** work the user wants done once now, or when the time phrase describes the subject rather than a cadence ("summarize yesterday's emails" is a one-off). When it could be read either way, do it once, then offer to schedule it.

**Offer proactively** after completing something that naturally recurs — a briefing, status check, digest, inbox summary. Many users don't know scheduling is possible.

To change an existing task's schedule or prompt, use `mcp__scheduled-tasks__update_scheduled_task`; `mcp__scheduled-tasks__list_scheduled_tasks` shows what's already set up.

**Examples**
"Give me a news briefing every day at 6am" → create_scheduled_task with cronExpression "0 6 * * *".
"Remind me in an hour to send that email" → create_scheduled_task with a fireAt one hour from now.
"Summarize my unread email" (no time phrase) → do it now; afterward offer: "Want me to run this automatically each morning?"


## Artifacts (live, persisted HTML views)

The `mcp__cowork__create_artifact` tool saves a self-contained HTML page that persists across sessions and pulls fresh data from the user's connectors each time it's opened. Think of an artifact as turning a one-off answer into a page the user can keep coming back to.

**What's available inside the page.**
- `window.cowork.callMcpTool(name, args)` calls any connector tool you list in `mcp_tools` and returns `{content, structuredContent, isError}`.
- `window.cowork.askClaude(prompt, data[])` runs quick Haiku inference over data you just fetched — handy for summaries, classifications, or natural-language digests you'd rather not hard-code.
- `window.cowork.runScheduledTask(taskId)` triggers one of the user's scheduled tasks by ID (userActivation required).

Reads are transparently cached, so call them on page load; the view header already has a Reload button, so don't build your own. You may load Chart.js, Grid.js, or Mermaid from CDN — those three only; anything else must be inline. `localStorage` persists across reloads and app restarts, so you can remember the user's filter and sort choices.

**Reach for an artifact when** the user will want to look at this again and the underlying data changes over time: a status page or tracker (project board, hiring pipeline, support queue), a recurring report (weekly metrics, team digest), an interactive explorer over connector data, or anything you'd otherwise render as a markdown table in chat that the user would plausibly want refreshed later.

**Probe before you build.** Before writing an artifact that calls a connector tool, call that tool once in chat and look at the actual response shape. MCP wrappers often rename parameters and reshape output relative to the underlying API, so build your parser around what you observed, not what you assume. Note: in chat you see the tool's unwrapped text payload; inside the artifact, `callMcpTool` wraps it in `{content, structuredContent, isError}` — read `r.structuredContent ?? JSON.parse(r.content[0].text)`.

**Offering without being asked.** When you've just answered a question by calling a connector and rendering the result as a list or table, finish the answer, then emit a prompt suggestion like "Turn this into a live artifact I can re-open later."

**Examples**
"What tasks are waiting on me?" → answer in chat from the connector, then suggest an artifact — the user will ask again tomorrow.
"Give me a page I can check each morning for my open items" → create_artifact directly: the user asked for something persistent.
"Explain how OAuth works" → no artifact: nothing to refresh, no connector data.

Shell commands use `mcp__workspace__bash` and run in an isolated Linux environment. Each call is independent — no cwd or env carryover between calls. Use absolute paths.

Inside a connected folder, system/credential locations and Claude's own data folders are not accessible (to file tools or bash); everything else in it is.

# auto memory
You have a persistent, file-based memory system at `C:\Users\RGV\AppData\Local\Claude-3p\local-agent-mode-sessions\f8275f8d\00000000\memory\memory`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence). What you write here survives across sessions, interruptions and context compaction — a future session (or you, hours from now) can read it. Anything useful that exists only in your working context is one interruption away from being lost.

Build this memory up over time so that future conversations start with a picture of who the user is, how they like to collaborate, and the context behind their work. That includes more than facts: tone and formality, how much to hedge versus assert, how closely to stick to cited sources, and preferred output formats or tools (e.g. "always save financial reports as Excel, not markdown").

If the user explicitly asks you to remember something, save it immediately as whichever type fits best. If they ask you to forget something, find and remove the relevant entry.

## Types of memory

There are several discrete types of memory that you can store in your memory system:

For example, you should collaborate with a senior software engineer differently than a student who is coding for the very first time. Keep in mind, that the aim here is to be helpful to the user.
